title: The missing variable in Africa’s industrial policy debate: political settlements
body:
Across African economies, governments are identifying strategic sectors, setting localization targets, and introducing incentives for critical minerals, and green transition technologies.

The debate that follows is usually the same: Which industrial policies should governments adopt?

But this is only part of the story. A more fundamental question is: Who decides which sectors receive support, and why?

Industrial policy is not simply about correcting market failures. It is about allocating scarce resources, opportunities, and rents. These decisions are rarely technical as I showed in "Policy Insights N43-2026" and "Policy Insights N13-2026".

Industrial policies and their outcomes are shaped by political settlements—the distribution of power among political elites, firms, bureaucracies, financiers, and other influential actors.

This is where the nature of the political settlement becomes decisive. PolicyInsights N43-2026 highlights two contrasting cases:

- A productive political settlement where state support is linked to credible performance obligations. Here, industrial policy is a mechanism for capability accumulation and structural transformation.
- A distributive political settlement where access to industrial support is determined largely by political proximity, patronage, or coalition maintenance. Here, the language is industrialization, but the outcome is rent distribution.
- But there is also a third possibility—an extractive political settlement where industrial policy is publicly embraced but never allowed to challenge the underlying economic structure. Here, policy changes at the level of rhetoric, but not at the level of accumulation.

These varieties means that the same industrial policy can produce very different outcomes.

This is particularly important in Africa’s current moment and requires asking one more question. Are industrial policies designed to transform the productive structure, or merely to preserve the existing political settlement?

**Implication:** The green transition has created a rare industrial window for Africa.

- But opportunity alone will not deliver transformation. That opportunity will also not be seized simply because governments identify priority sectors.
- The opportunity will be seized only where political coalitions are organized around production rather than patronage, capability rather than capture, and long-term transformation rather than short-term distribution.

**Bottom line:** Africa's industrial future will depend less on the sectors governments choose than on the coalitions, institutions, and power structures that shape those choices.

That is the debate we should be having. The challenge thus is not only to design better policies and identify priority sectors. It is to build good political settlements.
